title: Q&A with Climate Scientist David Victor, Part 1: Where Things Stand | Dimensional
gist: UC San Diego climate scientist David Victor argues the world has moved from a 4–5°C warming track to roughly 2.5–3°C, that the 1.5–2°C goals and the net-zero pledges built on them were never achievable, and that the honest downgrade of corporate climate targets ('blinking') is a positive, more investable development. He reads the current energy crisis as a Rorschach test in which the US doubles down on oil production while China, Europe and Japan accelerate efficiency, renewables and nuclear restarts.

insights.claim: The world's warming trajectory has improved from 4–5°C above preindustrial levels 15–20 years ago to roughly 2.5–3°C today, according to UC San Diego climate scientist David Victor.
insights.speaker: David Victor
insights.so_what: Tail-risk climate scenarios used in stress tests and catastrophe-linked pricing may be anchored to an outdated 4–5°C baseline; the central case has shifted materially cooler.
insights.quote: About 15–20 years ago, the world was on track for 4–5°C of warming above preindustrial levels. Right now we’re on track for maybe 2.5–3° of warming.
insights.locator: Victor: About 15–20 years ago

insights.claim: Victor argues progress on climate should be measured against the counterfactual trajectory (5°C avoided) rather than against the 1.5–2°C target, reframing an apparent failure as substantial success.
insights.speaker: David Victor
insights.so_what: A measurement frame that scores progress off the prior track rather than the aspirational target changes how climate-exposed assets and policy risk should be discounted.
insights.quote: I see this as good news: 2.5–3° is not 5°, and that’s the right way to measure progress.
insights.locator: I see this as good news

insights.claim: Global greenhouse gas emissions have not yet peaked, but the growth rate of global emissions has started to slow — a completely different picture from the soaring emissions of the early 2000s.
insights.speaker: David Victor
insights.so_what: Peak emissions is still ahead, so fossil demand does not collapse near-term; the inflection is in the second derivative, not the level.
insights.quote: Not enough to stop climate change, but a completely different picture from the early 2000s when emissions were soaring.
insights.locator: In terms of global emissions, we haven’t seen a peak

insights.claim: China remains by far the world's largest emitter, but its emissions growth has begun to level off, driven by an economic slowdown plus a shift toward renewables and more efficient coal plants.
insights.speaker: David Victor
insights.so_what: Part of China's emissions plateau is cyclical (GDP slowdown), not structural — a Chinese reacceleration could re-steepen the global emissions curve.
insights.locator: At the individual country level, China is

insights.claim: Total coal consumption in China has probably peaked, with new coal plants largely replacing older, less efficient units rather than adding net capacity.
insights.speaker: David Victor
insights.so_what: A peak in Chinese coal demand is the single largest swing factor for seaborne thermal coal markets and coal-linked equities.
insights.quote: They’re still building coal plants, but a lot of the new coal plants are replacing older plants that were not very efficient; total coal consumption in China has probably peaked.
insights.locator: They’re still building coal plants

insights.claim: China's electric vehicle build-out has plausibly cut Chinese oil consumption by more than a million barrels per day, according to David Victor.
insights.speaker: David Victor
insights.so_what: A >1 mb/d structural demand deletion from the world's largest oil importer is a direct headwind to long-dated crude demand forecasts and refiner margins.
insights.quote: There has also been an incredible build-out of electric vehicles, which has reduced Chinese oil consumption, plausibly by more than a million barrels a day.
insights.locator: There has also been an incredible build-out

insights.claim: In response to the current energy crisis, China has doubled down on efficiency, electric vehicles, renewables and nuclear rather than on conventional fossil supply.
insights.speaker: David Victor
insights.so_what: High energy prices are accelerating, not delaying, China's electrification capex — supportive for grid, nuclear and EV supply chains levered to Chinese demand.
insights.quote: And the Chinese have doubled down on efficiency, electric vehicles, renewables, and nuclear.
insights.locator: And the Chinese have doubled down

insights.claim: Emissions intensity — greenhouse gases per unit of economic output — has plummeted, meaning economic growth is being decoupled from pollution.
insights.speaker: David Victor
insights.so_what: Growth and emissions are no longer a fixed ratio, so GDP-linked emissions models used in transition scenarios systematically overstate future emissions.
insights.locator: Emissions intensity is a way to measure

insights.claim: When the decoupling data are decomposed, most of the improvement comes from energy efficiency — more economic output per unit of energy input — rather than from cleaner energy sources.
insights.speaker: David Victor
insights.so_what: Efficiency, not generation mix, is the dominant decarbonization lever to date, favoring industrial efficiency and demand-side technology over pure renewables exposure.
insights.quote: most of that decoupling is because of efficiency: The economy is much better at producing economic output per unit of energy input than in the past
insights.locator: And when you decompose those data

insights.claim: Victor ranks carbon intensity of energy sources as coal highest, natural gas lightest among fossil fuels, and renewables, nuclear and geothermal essentially zero — with US coal-to-gas switching cited as the exemplar of a large intensity reduction.
insights.speaker: David Victor
insights.so_what: Natural gas is framed as a legitimate decarbonization tool rather than a stranded asset, supporting gas infrastructure as a transition play.
insights.locator: Among fossil fuels, coal is the most carbon intensive

insights.claim: The US and Europe are experiencing 'shallow decarbonization,' with cheap natural gas and renewables displacing coal in the US.
insights.speaker: David Victor
insights.so_what: Developed-market emissions declines are the easy, price-driven kind; the hard, capital-intensive deep cuts have not begun.
insights.quote: What’s also interesting is that we’re seeing a shallow decarbonization in the US and Europe.
insights.locator: What’s also interesting is that we’re seeing

insights.claim: Victor holds the contrarian view that the 1.5–2°C warming targets were never achievable given how long energy systems take to change direction, and calls them climate policy goals disconnected from reality.
insights.speaker: David Victor
insights.so_what: Portfolios and mandates benchmarked to 1.5°C-aligned pathways are anchored to a scenario the author says was infeasible from the start.
insights.quote: These goals, which many policymakers still talk about a lot, are good examples of climate policy goals disconnected from reality.
insights.locator: We’re not on track for the 1.5–2°

insights.claim: Corporate and government pledges of 'net zero by 2030' or 'net zero by 2050' were derived from the 1.5–2°C targets, so their infeasibility propagates directly into company-level commitments now being discovered as unmeetable.
insights.speaker: David Victor
insights.so_what: Expect a wave of target revisions across corporates; screening on pledge existence rather than pledge feasibility is a flawed ESG signal.
insights.quote: Now nearly everyone is finding out how hard it is to meet those goals.
insights.locator: Still, many governments and companies set goals

insights.claim: Air New Zealand is cited as a company that has already 'blinked' — walking away from its climate goals and adopting new ones — which Victor calls a very good thing.
insights.speaker: David Victor
insights.so_what: First movers in target downgrades take reputational risk; if the practice normalizes, the penalty for honest revision shrinks and more firms follow.
insights.quote: Air New Zealand, for example, walked away from its goals and adopted new ones. I think this is a very good thing.
insights.locator: Companies have been worried about the repercussions

insights.claim: Victor argues companies have been suppressing admissions of missed climate goals out of fear of repercussions, implying that reported target compliance understates the true shortfall.
insights.speaker: David Victor
insights.so_what: Disclosed climate progress is likely biased optimistic; the information value is in which firms revise first and explain why.
insights.quote: Companies have been worried about the repercussions if they admit they can’t meet their goals, but we’ve started to see some firms “blink.”
insights.locator: Companies have been worried about the repercussions

insights.claim: Victor says we are at the beginning of a much more pragmatic theory of change in which policymakers and investors pursue what is feasible rather than promising the impossible — the argument of his December 27, 2025 New York Times opinion piece.
insights.speaker: David Victor
insights.so_what: A regime shift from aspirational to feasible targets changes which climate claims are credible and which transition capex actually gets funded.
insights.quote: I think we’re at the beginning of a much more pragmatic theory of change.
insights.locator: At the end of December, I wrote an opinion piece

insights.claim: What an individual company can achieve on emissions depends on the larger technological and policy ecosystem, not on corporate will alone — so company-level targets are partly exogenous.
insights.speaker: David Victor
insights.so_what: Judge a company's decarbonization on what its sector's technology and policy ecosystem permits, not on the ambition of its stated pledge.
insights.quote: what an individual company is able to achieve depends, frankly, on the larger technological and policy ecosystem
insights.locator: When companies walk away from aspirational goals

insights.claim: Only about a dozen countries account for 80% of global emissions, and all of them except Russia, Iran and Saudi Arabia are broadly sympathetic to the energy transition.
insights.speaker: David Victor
insights.so_what: Effective climate cooperation needs a small club, not universal consensus — meaning policy risk is concentrated in a handful of jurisdictions investors can track directly.
insights.quote: only about a dozen countries account for 80% of global emissions, and the vast majority of them—except Russia, Iran, and Saudi Arabia, which are in the carbon exporting business—are broadly sympathetic to the energy transition
insights.locator: What’s interesting is that only about a dozen countries

insights.claim: Victor's implied view is that the carbon-exporting states (Russia, Iran, Saudi Arabia) are the structural holdouts to the energy transition because their national business model is selling carbon.
insights.speaker: David Victor
insights.so_what: Petrostate resistance is economic, not ideological, so it will persist regardless of diplomacy — a durable floor under fossil supply politics.
insights.locator: which are in the carbon exporting business

insights.claim: Robust market pricing of carbon can help but will not on its own produce the disruptive technological change needed for 80% or 100% emissions cuts, so pricing must be paired with smart industrial policy.
insights.speaker: David Victor
insights.so_what: Deep-decarbonization winners will be picked partly by industrial policy allocation, not just by carbon price levels — follow the subsidy programs.
insights.quote: But they won’t on their own create the disruptive technological changes needed for big cuts in emissions—like 80% or even 100% cuts.
insights.locator: Robust market pricing mechanisms for carbon emissions

insights.claim: Europe's cap-and-trade emissions trading scheme is working well, creating powerful incentives both to decarbonize and to impose carbon border adjustments so European firms aren't undercut by competitors who don't pay carbon costs.
insights.speaker: David Victor
insights.so_what: Carbon border adjustments are a predictable consequence of a functioning carbon price — a rising tariff risk for carbon-intensive exporters into the EU.
insights.locator: The European example is very encouraging

insights.claim: Victor prefers carbon taxes over emissions trading because a tax is technically easier to design so that it sends firms a reliable signal about the cost of compliance.
insights.speaker: David Victor
insights.so_what: Price volatility in cap-and-trade markets is a design flaw, not a feature — relevant to anyone underwriting long-horizon projects against carbon price forecasts.
insights.locator: I favor carbon taxes over emissions trading

insights.claim: Carbon pricing functions not only as a market signal but as a credibility signal that a government is serious about decarbonization.
insights.speaker: David Victor
insights.so_what: Use the presence and durability of carbon pricing as a proxy for a jurisdiction's policy commitment when sizing transition-capex exposure there.
insights.quote: carbon pricing isn’t just a market signal but also a credibility signal—a sign that government is serious
insights.locator: Politically that is hard as well

insights.claim: Victor frames the current energy crisis as a Rorschach inkblot test in which each government reads its pre-existing priorities into the same high prices — making the crisis a window into political priorities rather than a common policy shock.
insights.speaker: David Victor
insights.so_what: Expect policy divergence, not convergence, from the same energy price shock — regional energy policy trades should be traded against each other, not as one theme.
insights.quote: The current crisis is like one of those Rorschach inkblot tests. Everyone is seeing in the inkblot what they want to see.
insights.locator: Victor: The current crisis is like one of those

insights.claim: The current US federal administration reads high oil prices as an argument for doubling down on domestic oil production, while China, Europe and Japan read the same prices as an argument for reducing dependence on conventional fossil fuels.
insights.speaker: David Victor
insights.so_what: US policy support is flowing to upstream oil while Asian and European support flows to electrification — a divergence trade across energy equity geographies.
insights.locator: The current US federal administration seems to see high oil prices

insights.claim: In March the president of the European Commission called Europe's turn away from nuclear power a huge mistake, and Europe is now focusing on more natural gas, more renewable power, more efficiency and a little more carbon capture and storage.
insights.speaker: David Victor
insights.so_what: An explicit top-level European reversal on nuclear is a policy catalyst for European nuclear supply chains and for gas import infrastructure.
insights.quote: In March, the president of the European Commission called Europe’s turn away from nuclear power a huge mistake
insights.locator: In March, the president of the European Commission

insights.claim: Europe's crisis response would produce an economy that is both cleaner and less dependent on imported energy, particularly from Russia but also from the Middle East.
insights.speaker: David Victor
insights.so_what: Energy security and decarbonization are aligned in Europe, so transition spending there is insulated from a swing in climate politics.
insights.locator: All that together would mean a cleaner economy

insights.claim: Japan's restart of nuclear reactors shut after Fukushima was already in progress and has been turbocharged by fear of continued dependence on imported oil and gas for power generation.
insights.speaker: David Victor
insights.so_what: Accelerated Japanese restarts subtract structurally from Japanese LNG and fuel-oil import demand, a bearish input for Asian LNG balances.
insights.quote: This restart was already in progress and has been turbocharged by the country’s fear of ongoing dependence on imported oil and gas for power generation.
insights.locator: The current crisis is also enabling the Japanese

insights.speaker: Dimensional Fund Advisors
insights.so_what: AI-driven power demand is being treated as a distinct, forthcoming topic — a signal that the data center load question is now central to institutional energy research.
insights.quote: Stay tuned for Part 2, where we will explore how the growth in energy usage by AI data centers is impacting energy demand and emissions.
insights.locator: Stay tuned for Part 2

insights.claim: David Victor provides consulting services to Dimensional Fund Advisors LP and is part of Dimensional's network of ESG researchers and academics, a disclosed commercial relationship.
insights.speaker: Dimensional Fund Advisors
insights.so_what: The pragmatic, anti-1.5°C framing is being channeled into an asset manager's ESG research process, suggesting how large managers may reset climate assumptions.
insights.quote: David Victor provides consulting services to Dimensional Fund Advisors LP.

insights.claim: The climate-club argument is grounded in William Nordhaus's work on climate clubs and free-riding published in the American Economic Review (2015 and 2019).
insights.speaker: Dimensional Fund Advisors
insights.so_what: The small-club cooperation thesis has formal economic backing, making it a durable framework rather than an off-hand remark.
